title: Fine-tuning, adapters, distillation, and when not to train
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to distinguish full fine-tuning, adapter-based training, and distillation, then decide whether training is appropriate for a specific model requirement. After completing it, learners can select an approach, explain the trade-offs, and design a baseline evaluation before committing training resources.
objectives: Distinguish full fine-tuning, adapter-based training, and knowledge distillation by identifying what is trained in each approach.
Decide whether a requirement calls for behavioral adaptation, external knowledge retrieval, model compression, or no model training.
Choose an evaluation baseline and held-out checks before comparing a trained model with its starting model.
Identify data, governance, and operational questions that must be resolved before training.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes familiarity with training examples, model inference, and the distinction between training data and held-out evaluation data. It does not assume knowledge of optimization mathematics or any provider-specific training system. In this module, fine-tuning means continuing training from an existing model by changing its trainable parameters for a target task or behavior. Full fine-tuning changes the original model parameters, while parameter-efficient approaches keep the original parameters fixed and train a smaller set of added or selected parameters. This distinction is described directly in the primary research on parameter-efficient transfer and low-rank adaptation [S1; S2].

sections.title: Start with the required change
paragraphs: Before selecting a training method, state the required change in observable terms. Examples include following a stable output format, applying a classification policy, answering from a changing document collection, or running a smaller model under a deployment constraint. This framing separates behavior changes, knowledge-access changes, and compression goals. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Do not begin with the assumption that training is required. Treat training as one possible intervention and compare it with simpler interventions that can satisfy the same acceptance test. If instructions or workflow controls already produce acceptable results, further training adds work without changing the decision outcome. If the requirement is access to information that changes independently of the model, consider retrieval rather than encoding that information through training. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies retrieved text to a generator and was introduced as a way to combine learned model parameters with an external document index [S4]. sections.title: Full fine-tuning
paragraphs: Full fine-tuning continues training while updating the original model parameters. The low-rank adaptation research contrasts this approach with freezing the original weights and training a much smaller set of added parameters [S2]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Consider full fine-tuning when the required behavioral change is broad enough to justify modifying the base model and when the team can evaluate, store, govern, and deploy the resulting model as a distinct trained artifact. This is a decision rule, not a guarantee that full fine-tuning will improve a particular task. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Do not infer success from training loss alone. Compare the resulting model with the unchanged baseline on held-out examples that represent the intended use, important failure cases, and unacceptable behavior. The evaluation should use the same tests for every candidate so that the intervention, rather than a changed test, explains the comparison. sections.title: Adapter-based training
paragraphs: Classic adapter training inserts small trainable modules into a pretrained network while keeping the original network parameters fixed. The original adapter research demonstrated this structure as a parameter-efficient alternative to training a separate full model for every task [S1]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Low-rank adaptation also freezes the existing model weights, but it represents the trainable change through low-rank matrices associated with selected layers. Its primary paper describes this method as reducing the number of trainable parameters relative to full fine-tuning [S2]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Use adapter-based training as a candidate when you want a learned behavior change but also want to preserve an unchanged base model. Confirm that the intended training and serving environment supports the chosen adapter approach before designing around it. No universal compatibility claim is made here. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Adapter-based training is not automatically the best choice merely because it trains fewer parameters. The correct comparison is whether it meets the same held-out quality requirements and operational constraints as the alternatives. sections.title: Knowledge distillation
paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using a teacher model's outputs as part of the training signal. The foundational distillation paper describes training the student with softened teacher output distributions, optionally combined with the ordinary labeled objective [S3]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Distillation is therefore aimed at transferring behavior into a separate student, commonly when the desired outcome is a model that is easier to deploy under a size or computation constraint. The student must still be evaluated independently because it is a newly trained model rather than a reference to the teacher at inference time [S3]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Teacher outputs are training targets in the distillation process, so the evaluation must include cases where the teacher is weak or wrong. A student that closely imitates an unwanted teacher behavior has not met the deployment requirement, even if the imitation objective improved. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. sections.title: How the approaches differ
paragraphs: The central distinction is what receives training updates. Full fine-tuning updates the original model parameters. Classic adapters keep those parameters fixed and train added modules. Low-rank adaptation keeps the original weights fixed and trains low-rank parameter changes. Distillation trains a separate student from a signal that includes teacher outputs [S1; S2; S3]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

The approaches also answer different design questions. Fine-tuning and adapter-based training ask how to adapt an existing model's behavior. Distillation asks how to train a student to reproduce useful aspects of a teacher. Retrieval asks how to provide external information during generation without relying only on information encoded in model parameters [S4]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

These categories can be combined in a larger system, but combination is not automatically beneficial. Each added intervention needs its own reason, acceptance test, and operational owner. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. sections.title: When not to train
paragraphs: Do not train when the requirement is not yet testable. If stakeholders cannot provide representative inputs, expected outcomes, and unacceptable outcomes, there is no reliable basis for deciding whether training helped. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Do not train merely to insert frequently changing facts. A retrieval design can supply external passages during generation, allowing the information source to remain separate from the model parameters [S4]. Evaluate whether retrieved passages are relevant and whether generated answers are supported by those passages. Do not train when a stable instruction, deterministic transformation, or workflow control already meets the acceptance test. In that case, training introduces another artifact to evaluate and govern without an established benefit. sections.title: A practical decision procedure
paragraphs: First, define an observable target and a held-out evaluation. Record the unchanged model's results as the baseline. Include ordinary cases, difficult cases, and cases that must not produce the requested behavior. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Second, identify the change type. For a behavior change, test instructions or workflow controls before considering fine-tuning or adapters. For changing external knowledge, test retrieval. For a smaller student that should imitate a teacher, test distillation. For a broad learned modification to the existing model, compare full fine-tuning with a parameter-efficient approach. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Third, list operational constraints before training. Include evaluation ownership, permitted data use, artifact storage, deployment compatibility, rollback, monitoring, and the process for replacing or retiring the trained artifact. The risk-management framework's Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage functions provide a first-party structure for organizing these responsibilities [S5]. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Fourth, compare candidates on the same held-out cases and acceptance thresholds. Select the least complex intervention that meets the requirement. If no candidate meets it, retain the baseline and revise the data, requirement, or evaluation rather than declaring success. sections.title: Evaluation and stop rules
paragraphs: Keep training examples separate from the final held-out comparison. Use the held-out set to compare the unchanged baseline, the trained candidate, and any non-training alternative under the same conditions. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. Measure what the requirement actually names. A formatting task needs format-validity checks. A classification task needs checks against expected labels and important error types. A retrieval-grounded task needs checks that the retrieved material is relevant and that the answer is supported by it. A compressed student needs comparison with both the teacher and the deployment constraints that motivated compression. In production environments, engineers must account for token utilization patterns, context window pressure, and deterministic execution boundaries. When system constraints or rate limits are approached, explicit retry strategies with exponential backoff and jitter prevent cascading failures across downstream dependencies.

Set stop rules before running the comparison. Stop if the candidate misses a required quality threshold, creates an unacceptable failure, cannot be deployed in the intended environment, or uses data that has not passed the required governance review. These rules prevent a favorable secondary metric from concealing failure on the actual requirement. sections.callout: A successful training run is not the same as a successful intervention. Success means beating the baseline on the declared acceptance test without violating a stop rule.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes classic adapter training from full fine-tuning?
choices: Classic adapter training keeps the original network parameters fixed and trains added modules, while full fine-tuning updates the original parameters.
Classic adapter training retrieves documents, while full fine-tuning stores documents outside the model.
Classic adapter training trains a separate student, while full fine-tuning never changes model parameters.
Classic adapter training requires no evaluation, while full fine-tuning requires held-out evaluation.
questions.explanation: Classic adapters add trainable modules while keeping the original network parameters fixed. Full fine-tuning updates the original model parameters [S1; S2].

questions.prompt: A team needs answers based on a document collection that changes every week. Which option should it test before trying to encode those facts through training?
choices: Full fine-tuning after every document change
Retrieval that supplies relevant external passages during generation
Distillation without access to the documents
Removing the held-out evaluation
questions.explanation: The module recommends testing retrieval when knowledge changes independently of the model because retrieval supplies external text during generation [S4].

questions.prompt: What is the defining training relationship in knowledge distillation?
choices: A student is trained using a signal that includes a teacher's outputs.
An unchanged model is connected to a document index without training.
All original model parameters are frozen and no other parameters are trained.
A validation set is copied into the training set.
questions.explanation: Knowledge distillation trains a student with a training signal that includes outputs from a teacher, such as softened output distributions [S3].

questions.prompt: When should a team postpone training according to this module?
choices: When it lacks representative evaluation cases and clear expected outcomes
Whenever the base model produces any correct answer
Whenever an adapter approach exists
Whenever the teacher and student are different sizes
questions.explanation: Without representative cases and expected outcomes, the team cannot determine whether training improved the required behavior.

questions.prompt: Which comparison best supports a training decision?
choices: Compare each candidate on a different set of examples.
Compare training loss without testing the unchanged model.
Compare the baseline, trained candidate, and non-training alternative on the same held-out cases.
Select the method that changes the most parameters.
questions.explanation: Using the same held-out cases keeps the acceptance test consistent across the unchanged baseline, the trained candidate, and any non-training alternative.
